subject: Medicine
summary: Osteoporosis is a systemic skeletal disease with low bone mass and microarchitectural deterioration, raising fracture risk. Diagnosis relies on bone mineral density and clinical risk factors.

sections.p: Osteoporosis is defined by a bone mineral density (BMD) T‑score ≤ ‑2.5 at the lumbar spine, hip, or forearm, or by a fragility fracture in the presence of low BMD.
b: BMD measured by DXA is the gold standard
Fracture history can diagnose even if DXA unavailable

t.b: What is the bone density? – A T‑score ≤ ‑2.5 confirms osteoporosis; ‑1 to ‑2.5 indicates osteopenia.

sections.p: Severity is staged by BMD T‑score and presence of fractures: osteopenia (‑1 to ‑2.5), osteoporosis (≤ ‑2.5), severe/established osteoporosis (≤ ‑2.5 with fragility fracture).
b: Fracture history upgrades severity
FRAX 10‑year risk >20% for major osteoporotic fracture is high risk

sections.p: Most cases are primary: post‑menopausal estrogen loss and age‑related bone loss. Secondary causes must be screened, especially in low‑resource settings.
b: Post‑menopausal estrogen deficiency
Age‑related senile bone loss
Chronic glucocorticoid use
Malabsorption (celiac, inflammatory bowel disease)
HIV infection or antiretroviral therapy
Chronic TB or vertebral TB causing localized loss
Rheumatic diseases with long‑term steroids

sections.p: Patients are often asymptomatic until a low‑impact fracture occurs, commonly at the vertebrae, hip, or distal radius.
b: Back pain from vertebral compression fracture
Loss of height or kyphosis
Hip pain after a fall from standing height

sections.p: Investigations confirm low bone density, assess fracture risk, and look for secondary causes.

t.b: Are bone turnover markers abnormal? – Normal calcium with high ALP may suggest high turnover disease.
Is vitamin D deficient? – <20 ng/mL indicates deficiency, which worsens bone loss.
Is hyperthyroidism present? – Low TSH can accelerate bone loss.
Is HIV infection a contributor? – HIV and some antiretrovirals increase fracture risk.

sections.p: Complications include painful vertebral fractures, hip fractures, and secondary spinal cord compression.
b: Sudden back pain with height loss – possible vertebral fracture
Inability to bear weight after a fall – possible hip fracture
Progressive kyphosis causing respiratory compromise

sections.p: Treat underlying causes, ensure adequate calcium/vitamin D, and start anti‑resorptive therapy. Lifestyle measures support bone health.
b: Calcium 1000‑1200 mg/day from diet or supplements
Vitamin D 800‑1000 IU/day (or higher if deficient)
Bisphosphonates (e.g., alendronate) – inhibit osteoclasts, reduce fracture risk
Denosumab for renal impairment or intolerance to bisphosphonates – RANKL inhibitor
Avoid long‑term steroids if possible; switch to steroid‑sparing agents

sections.p: Re‑measure BMD every 1‑2 years, monitor adherence, and reinforce fall‑prevention strategies.
b: DXA repeat at 2 years if on therapy, sooner if fracture occurs
Assess fall risk: vision, home hazards, muscle strength
Encourage weight‑bearing exercise (walking, resistance training)

sections.p: Conditions that also cause bone pain or fractures can be mistaken for osteoporosis.
b: Osteomalacia – low vitamin D causing soft bones, labs show low calcium/phosphate
Paget disease – focal bone enlargement, high ALP
Metastatic bone disease – lytic lesions on imaging

sections.p: Certain factors may mask true bone health.
b: Obesity can give falsely high BMD despite poor bone quality
Degenerative spinal changes can overestimate lumbar spine BMD
Recent vertebral fracture may lower BMD, exaggerating severity

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe back pain after a minor fall
Inability to stand or walk after a fall
Progressive loss of height or new kyphosis

faq.a: Yes, especially after age 70 or with risk factors like steroids, low testosterone, or chronic disease.

faq.q: Is calcium alone enough to prevent fractures?
faq.a: No, calcium must be combined with vitamin D and, when indicated, anti‑resorptive medication.
They have strong evidence for reducing vertebral and hip fractures and are inexpensive.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A focused history and targeted physical exam identify fracture risk, secondary causes and the presence of silent vertebral fractures, while recognising the limits of bedside assessment.
b: Age, sex, menopausal status and any prior low‑impact fractures
Medication history: glucocorticoids, anticonvulsants, ART, TB therapy, chronic NSAIDs
Dietary calcium/vitamin D intake, alcohol use, smoking, physical activity
Symptoms of vertebral fracture: acute back pain, height loss, kyphosis
Systemic clues to secondary causes: chronic diarrhoea, malabsorption, recurrent infections, joint pain, renal disease
Family history of early fractures or rare bone disease
Menstrual history and pregnancy status in women of reproductive age

t.a: Inspection for kyphosis or height loss
t.b: Detects chronic vertebral compression; a visible thoracic hump or >4 cm loss of height suggests multiple fractures; bedside cannot quantify fracture severity
Tenderness over a vertebra indicates acute compression fracture; pain localized to one level is typical; cannot differentiate osteoporotic from traumatic fracture
Impaired balance raises fall risk; inability to stand >30 seconds signals high fracture risk; does not measure bone density
Excludes rheumatoid arthritis or osteoarthritis as secondary contributors; joint deformities do not confirm osteoporosis

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Use available tests to confirm low bone mass, quantify fracture risk and uncover secondary causes; adapt when DXA or labs are not accessible.
b: DXA of lumbar spine and hip: T‑score ≤‑2.5 confirms osteoporosis; T‑score between ‑1 and ‑2.5 is osteopenia; Z‑score ≤‑2 in <50 y suggests secondary cause
FRAX (clinical risk factors ± BMD): 10‑yr major fracture risk >20 % = high risk; >10 % = moderate; guides treatment threshold
Serum calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase: low calcium or high ALP may indicate malabsorption or metabolic bone disease
25‑OH vitamin D: <20 ng/mL = deficiency, <12 ng/mL = severe; replete before anti‑resorptives
Renal function (eGFR): <30 mL/min/1.73 m² contraindicates bisphosphonates; adjust dosing
CBC, ESR/CRP: anemia or elevated inflammatory markers raise suspicion for chronic disease, TB or HIV
Thyroid function, cortisol (AM), testosterone/estradiol: abnormal values point to endocrine secondary causes

t.b: Use quantitative ultrasound of the calcaneus (T‑score ≤‑2.5 equivalent) or rely on clinical fracture history plus FRAX without BMD
Apply WHO clinical criteria: age ≥ 65 y (women) or ≥ 70 y (men) with prior fragility fracture = treatment indication

sections.p: Classification integrates bone density, fracture history and risk calculators to guide management intensity.
b: Osteopenia: T‑score –1.0 to –2.5, no fragility fracture
Osteoporosis: T‑score ≤‑2.5 at lumbar spine, hip or forearm
Severe osteoporosis: T‑score ≤‑2.5 plus one or more fragility fractures
Very severe osteoporosis: T‑score ≤‑2.5 plus multiple vertebral fractures or hip fracture
High FRAX risk: ≥20 % 10‑yr major osteoporotic fracture or ≥3 % hip fracture
Secondary osteoporosis: Z‑score ≤‑2 in patients <50 y or identified cause (e.g., glucocorticoids)

sections.p: Conditions that mimic low BMD or cause similar fractures must be distinguished by history, labs and imaging.

t.b: Bone pain, muscle weakness, low vitamin D, raised ALP; X‑ray shows Looser’s zones; normal or low BMD but poor mineralisation distinguishes it
Back pain, anemia, hypercalcaemia, renal failure; serum protein electrophoresis shows monoclonal spike; lytic lesions on skeletal survey differentiate
Enlarged bone, hearing loss, high ALP, mosaic pattern on radiograph; BMD may be high locally, not low overall
Elevated PTH, low calcium, high phosphate; bone biopsy shows high‑turnover disease; DXA may be low but context is renal

sections.p: Begin with risk assessment, then initiate first‑line therapy, monitor response, and decide when to intensify or refer.
b: Assess fracture risk with FRAX; if >20% major fracture, treat immediately.
Start oral bisphosphonate (e.g., alendronate) as first‑line; avoid if severe renal impairment.
If no response or intolerance, switch to intravenous bisphosphonate or denosumab.
Add calcium (800–1000 mg/day) and vitamin D (800–1000 IU/day) to all patients.
Re‑measure BMD at 1–2 years; if T‑score remains ≤‑2.5 or new fracture, consider anabolic agent.
Refer to specialist if renal failure, severe hypocalcaemia, or atypical femoral fracture occurs.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Monitor for common adverse effects and drug interactions, acting promptly to prevent complications.
b: GI irritation: advise taking with water, upright for 30 min, and a light meal; if persistent, switch to oral or IV formulation.
Hypocalcaemia: check serum calcium before and after therapy; supplement if low.
Atypical femoral fractures: counsel on pain and stop bisphosphonate if prodromal pain appears.
Osteonecrosis of jaw: ensure dental clearance before therapy; treat dental issues promptly.
Drug interactions: avoid concurrent use of proton pump inhibitors or calcium‑rich supplements within 4 h of bisphosphonate.

sections.p: Recognise red flags that warrant urgent action or specialist input.
b: New vertebral collapse with severe back pain: urgent imaging and possible surgical referral.
Hip fracture after minimal trauma: immediate orthopaedic assessment and surgical fixation.
Unexplained weight loss or night sweats: evaluate for malignancy or TB.
Severe renal dysfunction (eGFR <30 ml/min): discontinue bisphosphonate and consider alternative therapy.
Persistent hypocalcaemia despite supplementation: investigate vitamin D deficiency or parathyroid dysfunction.

sections.p: These conditions alter presentation, diagnostics, or treatment choices.
b: HIV: antiretroviral therapy can accelerate bone loss; monitor BMD closely and consider anabolic agents.
TB: chronic infection and steroids increase fracture risk; treat TB aggressively before starting bisphosphonate.
Malnutrition: low protein and micronutrients worsen bone quality; provide dietary counselling and supplements.
Pregnancy: avoid bisphosphonates; use calcium and vitamin D only; treat underlying causes.
Diabetes: poor glycaemic control impairs bone healing; optimise glucose levels.
Herbal remedies: some (e.g., ginseng) may interfere with bisphosphonate absorption; review all supplements.
Alcohol: chronic intake reduces bone formation; counsel abstinence and provide calcium/vitamin D.
Renal or hepatic failure: dose adjust or avoid bisphosphonates; use denosumab if renal function is poor.

sections.p: Tailor management to unique physiological and resource constraints.
b: Children: focus on growth plate protection; avoid bisphosphonates unless severe disease; monitor growth charts.
Pregnancy: use calcium/vitamin D only; defer bisphosphonate until postpartum.
Elderly: prefer denosumab if renal impairment; monitor for falls and fractures.
HIV patients: integrate bone health into ART follow‑up; consider anabolic therapy if severe loss.
Low‑resource settings: use oral bisphosphonate as first line; rely on clinical fracture history when DXA unavailable; ensure calcium/vitamin D supplementation.

facts: Osteoporosis diagnosis: DXA T‑score ≤ -2.5 at lumbar spine, total hip or femoral neck.
FRAX 10‑year major osteoporotic fracture risk >20% = high risk.
Primary causes: post‑menopausal estrogen loss and age‑related bone loss.
Secondary causes to screen: chronic glucocorticoids, malabsorption, HIV/ART, TB, rheumatic disease.
First‑line pharmacologic therapy: oral bisphosphonate (alendronate) – inhibits osteoclast‑mediated bone resorption.
Adequate calcium intake: 1000 mg/day (women <50 yr) or 1200 mg/day (women ≥50 yr).
Vitamin D target: 25‑OH D ≥30 ng/mL (≥75 nmol/L).
Key bedside sign of vertebral fracture: loss of height >2 cm or kyphotic angle >15°.
Contra‑indication for oral bisphosphonates: esophageal stricture, inability to remain upright 30 min.

vivas.q: What is the WHO definition of osteoporosis?
vivas.a: A BMD T‑score ≤ -2.5 at the lumbar spine, hip or forearm measured by DXA.

vivas.q: How would you diagnose osteoporosis in a 68‑year‑old woman with a recent wrist fracture if DXA is unavailable?
vivas.a: A low‑impact fragility fracture in a woman >50 yr is sufficient for a clinical diagnosis of osteoporosis.

vivas.q: Name three secondary causes that must be screened for in a low‑resource setting.
vivas.a: Chronic glucocorticoid use, malabsorption (celiac/IBD), and HIV infection or antiretroviral therapy.

vivas.q: What is the pharmacokinetic property of alendronate that requires patients to stay upright after ingestion?
vivas.a: Poor oral absorption and high affinity for hydroxyapatite cause esophageal irritation; remaining upright reduces reflux risk.

vivas.q: Explain the pharmacodynamic mechanism of alendronate.
vivas.a: Alendronate binds to bone mineral and is taken up by osteoclasts, inhibiting farnesyl‑pyrophosphate synthase, leading to osteoclast apoptosis and reduced bone resorption.

vivas.q: Which cellular imbalance underlies post‑menopausal osteoporosis?
vivas.a: Increased osteoclast activity relative to osteoblast formation due to estrogen deficiency.

vivas.q: What is the primary mechanism by which bisphosphonates inhibit bone resorption?
vivas.a: Inhibition of farnesyl‑pyrophosphate synthase in the mevalonate pathway, causing osteoclast apoptosis.

vivas.q: A 25‑year‑old with short stature, cataracts, premature greying and osteoporosis – which enzyme class is mutated?
vivas.a: A lysosomal enzyme (α‑L‑iduronidase) causing mucopolysaccharidosis type I (Hurler syndrome).

vivas.q: Which demographic group has the highest overall risk for osteoporosis?
vivas.a: Post‑menopausal women, especially of Asian or Caucasian ethnicity.

vivas.q: List baseline laboratory investigations for osteoporosis and typical abnormal findings.
vivas.a: CBC (rule out anemia), serum calcium (low/normal), phosphate (low/normal), alkaline phosphatase (elevated if high turnover), 25‑OH vitamin D (deficient <30 ng/mL), renal function (creatinine), thyroid function (TSH), and fasting glucose/HbA1c (diabetes).

vivas.q: Describe the bedside examination steps to detect a vertebral compression fracture.
vivas.a: Inspect for kyphosis, measure height loss >2 cm, palpate spinous processes for tenderness, perform Adam’s forward bend test for localized pain, and assess for rib‑cage restriction.

vivas.q: Why is a plain lateral spine X‑ray preferred over DXA in an acute fracture setting?
vivas.a: It visualises fracture morphology, vertebral height loss and kyphosis, which DXA cannot detect in the acute phase.

vivas.q: When should you refer a patient with osteoporosis to orthopaedics?
vivas.a: If there is a hip fracture, progressive vertebral collapse causing neurological compromise, or failure of medical therapy after 2 years.

vivas.q: What non‑pharmacological measures reduce fracture risk?
vivas.a: Adequate calcium/vitamin D, weight‑bearing exercise, smoking cessation, limiting alcohol (<2 units/day), fall‑prevention strategies (home safety, vision correction).

vivas.q: How does chronic glucocorticoid use cause secondary osteoporosis?
vivas.a: It decreases osteoblastogenesis, increases osteoblast apoptosis, and enhances renal calcium loss, leading to net bone loss.

vivas.q: What is the significance of a FRAX 10‑year hip fracture risk ≥3%?
vivas.a: It meets treatment threshold for most guidelines, prompting initiation of anti‑resorptive therapy.

mcqs.q: A 70‑year‑old woman presents after a fall from standing height with hip pain. DXA is unavailable. Which finding alone justifies a diagnosis of osteoporosis?
mcqs.e: A fragility fracture in an older adult is diagnostic even without BMD measurement.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is the most common adverse effect that requires patients to remain upright for 30 minutes after taking alendronate?
mcqs.e: Oral bisphosphonates can cause esophagitis; upright posture reduces contact time.

mcqs.q: A 55‑year‑old post‑menopausal woman has a T‑score of -2.6 and a FRAX major osteoporotic fracture risk of 12%. Which next step is most appropriate?
o: Observe and repeat DXA in 5 years
mcqs.e: T‑score ≤ -2.5 meets treatment threshold regardless of FRAX; start bisphosphonate.

mcqs.q: Which laboratory test is most useful to exclude secondary hyperparathyroidism as a cause of low bone density?
mcqs.e: Elevated PTH with normal/low calcium suggests secondary hyperparathyroidism.

mcqs.q: In a patient with HIV on protease inhibitors, which factor most increases osteoporosis risk?
o: Direct effect of HIV on osteoclasts
mcqs.e: HIV infection itself and some ART agents increase bone turnover.

mcqs.q: Which sign on physical exam suggests a recent vertebral compression fracture?
mcqs.e: Loss of lumbar lordosis and kyphosis are typical of vertebral fractures.

cases.v: A 68‑year‑old Kenyan woman presents with sudden mid‑back pain after bending to pick up a child. She reports a 4 cm loss of height over the past year. Examination shows a palpable step‑off at T12 and a forward‑bending kyphosis. Lateral spine X‑ray shows 30 % anterior height loss of T12.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a: Acute osteoporotic vertebral compression fracture at T12.

qs.q: What immediate management steps should be taken?
qs.a: Analgesia, brace or orthosis for spinal support, calcium/vitamin D supplementation, and start oral bisphosphonate if no contraindication.

qs.q: Which investigation would you order if DXA is not available?
qs.a: FRAX calculation using clinical risk factors; if high risk, treat as osteoporosis.

mistakes: Confusing a T‑score of -1.8 as osteoporosis – it is osteopenia unless a fragility fracture is present.
Prescribing bisphosphonates without correcting severe vitamin D deficiency, risking hypocalcaemia.
Failing to ask about glucocorticoid use, which changes treatment thresholds.
Assuming a normal calcium level rules out secondary causes – PTH and vitamin D must still be checked.
Not advising patients to stay upright after oral bisphosphonate, leading to esophagitis.
Relying solely on DXA in acute vertebral fracture; plain radiograph is needed for fracture confirmation.
Neglecting fall‑risk assessment in the elderly, missing a key preventive step.
Using calcium supplements alone without vitamin D, which limits absorption.
